name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_SEQ_Q01 - Increasing order of reducing power of metals

questiontext.text:
Given the standard electrode potentials at \(298\text{ K}\):

  • \(\mathrm{Ag}^{+}/\mathrm{Ag} = +0.80\text{ V}\)
  • \(\mathrm{Hg}^{2+}/\mathrm{Hg} = +0.79\text{ V}\)
  • \(\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}/\mathrm{Cr} = -0.74\text{ V}\)
  • \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}/\mathrm{Mg} = -2.37\text{ V}\)
  • \(\mathrm{K}^{+}/\mathrm{K} = -2.93\text{ V}\)

Arrange these metals in the increasing order of their reducing power:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The standard electrode potential (\(E^{\ominus}\)) measures the tendency of the oxidised form to get reduced. A lower (more negative) \(E^{\ominus}\) value means the reduced form (metal) loses electrons more readily and is therefore a stronger reducing agent.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Metal
Comparing the given \(E^{\ominus}\) values from highest (most positive) to lowest (most negative):
\(+0.80\text{ V}\ (\mathrm{Ag}^{+}/\mathrm{Ag}) > +0.79\text{ V}\ (\mathrm{Hg}^{2+}/\mathrm{Hg}) > -0.74\text{ V}\ (\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}/\mathrm{Cr}) > -2.37\text{ V}\ (\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}/\mathrm{Mg}) > -2.93\text{ V}\ (\mathrm{K}^{+}/\mathrm{K})\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Since reducing power increases as \(E^{\ominus}\) decreases, the increasing order of reducing power is: \(\mathrm{Ag} < \mathrm{Hg} < \mathrm{Cr} < \mathrm{Mg} < \mathrm{K}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_SEQ_Q02 - Chronological steps to measure molar conductivity

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following experimental and computational steps in the correct chronological sequence to determine the molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_{m}\)) of an unknown aqueous electrolyte solution of known molarity \(c\):

(P) Measure the resistance \(R_{\mathrm{KCl}}\) of the conductivity cell filled with a standard \(\mathrm{KCl}\) solution of known conductivity \(\kappa_{\mathrm{KCl}}\).
(Q) Calculate the cell constant using \(G^{*} = R_{\mathrm{KCl}} \times \kappa_{\mathrm{KCl}}\).
(R) Fill the same conductivity cell with the unknown electrolyte solution and measure its resistance \(R\) using an AC Wheatstone bridge.
(S) Compute the conductivity \(\kappa = \frac{G^{*}}{R}\) and then molar conductivity \(\Lambda_{m} = \frac{\kappa \times 1000}{c}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Because direct measurement of the distance between electrodes (\(l\)) and their cross-sectional area (\(A\)) is inconvenient and unreliable, a conductivity cell must first be calibrated using a standard \(\mathrm{KCl}\) solution of accurately known conductivity before measuring the unknown solution.

Step 2: Logical Sequence of Operations
First, the resistance \(R_{\mathrm{KCl}}\) of the cell containing standard \(\mathrm{KCl}\) solution is measured. Second, the cell constant is determined from \(G^{*} = R_{\mathrm{KCl}} \times \kappa_{\mathrm{KCl}}\). Third, the cell is filled with the unknown electrolyte solution and its resistance \(R\) is measured using an AC Wheatstone bridge. Fourth, the conductivity \(\kappa = \frac{G^{*}}{R}\) is calculated and divided by the molarity \(c\) (with appropriate unit factor \(1000\)) to obtain \(\Lambda_{m}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence is: measuring \(R_{\mathrm{KCl}}\) \(\rightarrow\) calculating \(G^{*}\) \(\rightarrow\) measuring \(R\) of the unknown solution \(\rightarrow\) computing \(\kappa\) and \(\Lambda_{m}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_SEQ_Q03 - Chronological stages in electrochemical rusting of iron

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following events occurring during the atmospheric rusting of iron in the correct chronological sequence:

(P) Iron atoms lose electrons at an anodic spot to form \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq})\) ions.
(Q) Released electrons move through the iron metal to a cathodic spot.
(R) Atmospheric oxygen is reduced in the presence of \(\mathrm{H}^{+}\) ions to form water.
(S) Ferrous ions (\(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\)) are further oxidised by atmospheric oxygen to ferric ions, forming rust (\(\mathrm{Fe}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3}\cdot x\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\)).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Corrosion of iron in the presence of air and moisture operates as a miniature electrochemical cell on the metal surface, followed by atmospheric oxidation of ferrous ions to rust.

Step 2: Logical Sequence of Events
Initially, at an anodic spot on the iron surface, iron is oxidised: \(2\mathrm{Fe(s)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{e}^{-}\). Next, the released electrons conduct through the metallic iron to another spot acting as the cathode. There, oxygen is reduced in the presence of \(\mathrm{H}^{+}\) ions (from dissolved \(\mathrm{CO}_{2}\) or acidic oxides): \(\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)}\). Finally, the \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) ions are further oxidised by atmospheric oxygen to ferric ions, which precipitate as hydrated ferric oxide (\(\mathrm{Fe}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3}\cdot x\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\)), commonly known as rust.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence is: oxidation of \(\mathrm{Fe}\) to \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) \(\rightarrow\) electron conduction through iron \(\rightarrow\) reduction of \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\) to \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\) \(\rightarrow\) atmospheric oxidation of \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) to \(\mathrm{Fe}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3}\cdot x\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_SEQ_Q04 - Displacement order of metals from salt solutions

questiontext.text: Using the standard reduction potentials at \(298\text{ K}\) (\(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}/\mathrm{Mg} = -2.36\text{ V}\), \(\mathrm{Al}^{3+}/\mathrm{Al} = -1.66\text{ V}\), \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}/\mathrm{Zn} = -0.76\text{ V}\), \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}/\mathrm{Fe} = -0.44\text{ V}\), \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu} = +0.34\text{ V}\)), arrange the metals in the order in which each metal displaces the next one from an aqueous solution of its salt (from strongest displacing metal to weakest):

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A metal with a lower (more negative) standard reduction potential is a stronger reducing agent and can displace any metal with a higher (more positive) standard reduction potential from an aqueous solution of its salt.

Step 2: Evaluation of Standard Potentials
Ordering the \(E^{\ominus}\) values from lowest (most negative) to highest (most positive):
\(-2.36\text{ V}\ (\mathrm{Mg}) < -1.66\text{ V}\ (\mathrm{Al}) < -0.76\text{ V}\ (\mathrm{Zn}) < -0.44\text{ V}\ (\mathrm{Fe}) < +0.34\text{ V}\ (\mathrm{Cu})\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Magnesium can displace aluminium, aluminium can displace zinc, zinc can displace iron, and iron can displace copper from their respective salt solutions. Thus, the order is \(\mathrm{Mg}, \mathrm{Al}, \mathrm{Zn}, \mathrm{Fe}, \mathrm{Cu}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_SEQ_Q05 - Increasing order of conductivity of selected materials

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following materials and aqueous solutions in the increasing order of their electrical conductivity (\(\kappa\)) at \(298.15\text{ K}\):

Glass, Pure water, \(0.01\text{ M KCl(aq)}\), \(0.1\text{ M HCl(aq)}\), Copper

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Insulators have negligible conductivity, pure water has very low ionic conductivity due to auto-ionisation (\(\sim 10^{-7}\text{ M}\)), aqueous electrolytes have moderate ionic conductivity depending on concentration and ion mobility, and metals have very high electronic conductivity.

Step 2: Comparison of Conductivity Values at \(298.15\text{ K}\)
1. Glass (insulator): \(1.0 \times 10^{-16}\text{ S m}^{-1}\)
2. Pure water: \(3.5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ S m}^{-1}\)
3. \(0.01\text{ M KCl(aq)}\): \(0.14\text{ S m}^{-1}\)
4. \(0.1\text{ M HCl(aq)}\): \(3.91\text{ S m}^{-1}\) (higher concentration and highly mobile \(\mathrm{H}^{+}\) ions)
5. Copper (metallic conductor): \(5.9 \times 10^{3}\text{ S m}^{-1}\)

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The increasing order of conductivity is: Glass < Pure water < \(0.01\text{ M KCl(aq)}\) < \(0.1\text{ M HCl(aq)}\) < Copper.

answer.text: Pure water < Glass < \(0.01\text{ M KCl(aq)}\) < \(0.1\text{ M HCl(aq)}\) < Copper
Glass < Pure water < \(0.1\text{ M HCl(aq)}\) < \(0.01\text{ M KCl(aq)}\) < Copper
Glass < Pure water < \(0.01\text{ M KCl(aq)}\) < \(0.1\text{ M HCl(aq)}\) < Copper
Copper < \(0.1\text{ M HCl(aq)}\) < \(0.01\text{ M KCl(aq)}\) < Pure water < Glass

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_SEQ_Q06 - Sequence for determining dissociation constant of a weak acid

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following steps in the correct logical sequence to determine the dissociation constant (\(K_{a}\)) of a weak monobasic acid \(\mathrm{HA}\) at concentration \(c\):

(P) Measure the conductivity \(\kappa\) of the \(\mathrm{HA}\) solution of concentration \(c\) and calculate \(\Lambda_{m} = \frac{\kappa \times 1000}{c}\).
(Q) Calculate \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{HA})\) using Kohlrausch law from strong electrolytes: \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{HCl}) + \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NaA}) - \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NaCl})\).
(R) Compute the degree of dissociation using \(\alpha = \frac{\Lambda_{m}}{\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}}\).
(S) Substitute \(\alpha\) and \(c\) into \(K_{a} = \frac{c\alpha^{2}}{1-\alpha}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For a weak electrolyte, \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}\) cannot be obtained by extrapolation of \(\Lambda_{m}\) versus \(c^{1/2}\), so Kohlrausch law of independent migration of ions is combined with conductivity measurement at concentration \(c\) to find \(\alpha\) and \(K_{a}\).

Step 2: Logical Sequence of Calculation
First, the conductivity \(\kappa\) at concentration \(c\) is measured and converted to molar conductivity \(\Lambda_{m} = \frac{\kappa \times 1000}{c}\). Second, \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{HA})\) is obtained using Kohlrausch law by combining \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}\) values of strong electrolytes: \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{HCl}) + \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NaA}) - \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NaCl})\). Third, the degree of dissociation \(\alpha = \frac{\Lambda_{m}}{\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}}\) is computed from both values. Fourth, \(\alpha\) and \(c\) are substituted into the equilibrium expression \(K_{a} = \frac{c\alpha^{2}}{1-\alpha}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence is: finding \(\Lambda_{m}\) \(\rightarrow\) finding \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}\) via Kohlrausch law \(\rightarrow\) computing \(\alpha\) \(\rightarrow\) calculating \(K_{a}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_SEQ_Q07 - Increasing order of oxidising power of redox species

questiontext.text:
Given the standard reduction potentials at \(298\text{ K}\):

  • \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu} = +0.34\text{ V}\)
  • \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}/\mathrm{Fe}^{2+} = +0.77\text{ V}\)
  • \(\mathrm{Ag}^{+}/\mathrm{Ag} = +0.80\text{ V}\)
  • \(\mathrm{Br}_{2}/\mathrm{Br}^{-} = +1.09\text{ V}\)
  • \(\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}/\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\) (acidic) \(= +1.51\text{ V}\)

Arrange the oxidised species in the increasing order of their oxidising power:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a reduction half-reaction (\(\text{Oxidised form} + n\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Reduced form}\)), a higher (more positive) standard reduction potential \(E^{\ominus}\) indicates a greater tendency for the oxidised species to accept electrons and get reduced, meaning stronger oxidising power.

Step 2: Comparison of Standard Reduction Potentials
Arranging the \(E^{\ominus}\) values in increasing order:
\(+0.34\text{ V}\ (\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}) < +0.77\text{ V}\ (\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}) < +0.80\text{ V}\ (\mathrm{Ag}^{+}) < +1.09\text{ V}\ (\mathrm{Br}_{2}) < +1.51\text{ V}\ (\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-})\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the increasing order of oxidising power is: \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} < \mathrm{Fe}^{3+} < \mathrm{Ag}^{+} < \mathrm{Br}_{2} < \mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}\).
